title: Azure Site Recovery: replication and failover
learningObjective: Configure Azure-to-Azure replication with Site Recovery, run test failovers, fail over to a secondary region, commit, re-protect and fail back.
foundation: Site Recovery keeps a continuously updated copy of your VMs in another region. If the primary region fails, you fail over and run the VMs there within minutes.
A test failover proves it works without affecting production.
engineer: Set up: create a Recovery Services vault in the target region (not the source); enable replication from the VM (Disaster recovery) or the vault: target region, resource group, VNet/subnet, availability options, cache storage account in the source region, replication policy (recovery point retention up to 15 days, app-consistent snapshot frequency). The Mobility service extension is installed on the VMs.
Network mapping maps source VNets to target VNets. Recovery plans group VMs into ordered groups with scripts/manual actions for multi-tier apps.
Test failover: choose a recovery point and an isolated VNet; validate; then Cleanup test failover.

Failover: choose a recovery point (Latest = lowest RPO, processes pending data; Latest processed = lowest RTO; Latest app-consistent; Custom). Then Commit (discards other recovery points), Re-protect (replicate from the secondary back to the primary), and later fail back the same way.
RPO: how much data you can lose; RTO: how long recovery takes. Site Recovery targets low RPO (continuous replication) for Azure VMs.

example.title: Quarterly DR drill
body: Every quarter, the team runs a test failover of the recovery plan 'erp' into vnet-dr-test in West US, runs smoke tests, then cleans up. During a real East US outage they failed over with Latest processed, committed, and re-protected once East US recovered, failing back a week later.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription with VMs to monitor or protect
permissions: Site Recovery Contributor on the vault plus VM Contributor at source and target
limits: Recovery point retention up to 15 days
Vault must be in a region other than the source region
portal: VM > Disaster recovery: target region, advanced settings (resource group, VNet, cache storage, replication policy), Start replication.
Vault > Replicated items: monitor status until Protected.
Replicated item > Test failover > Cleanup test failover.
configuration.cli:
# Azure CLI support for Site Recovery is limited (az site-recovery extension); the portal and PowerShell are typical
az backup vault create -g rg-dr -n rsv-dr-wus -l westus
az extension add --name site-recovery
az site-recovery fabric list -g rg-dr --vault-name rsv-dr-wus
configuration.powershell:
$v = New-AzRecoveryServicesVault -ResourceGroupName rg-dr -Name rsv-dr-wus -Location westus
Set-AzRecoveryServicesAsrVaultContext -Vault $v
$fab = Get-AzRecoveryServicesAsrFabric
$rpi = Get-AzRecoveryServicesAsrReplicationProtectedItem -ProtectionContainer (Get-AzRecoveryServicesAsrProtectionContainer -Fabric $fab[0])
Start-AzRecoveryServicesAsrTestFailoverJob -ReplicationProtectedItem $rpi[0] -Direction PrimaryToRecovery -AzureVMNetworkId $testVnetId
Start-AzRecoveryServicesAsrUnplannedFailoverJob -ReplicationProtectedItem $rpi[0] -Direction PrimaryToRecovery
Start-AzRecoveryServicesAsrCommitFailoverJob -ReplicationProtectedItem $rpi[0]

steps: Run the default (vault in the source region).
Apply 'Vault in the target region' and read the next missing step.
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: Can't select the source region's vault.
troubleshooting.cause: A2A vault must be in another region.
troubleshooting.fix: Create the vault in the target region.

troubleshooting.symptom: Failed-over VMs can't reach each other.
troubleshooting.cause: No network mapping or wrong subnet.
troubleshooting.fix: Configure network mapping and recovery plan order.

comparisons.difference: Restores from backups (higher RPO/RTO); Site Recovery replicates continuously.
AWS equivalent for continuous replication and failover.

misconceptions.reality: It runs in an isolated network; production keeps running.
It doesn't keep long-term history; use both.

architectureDecisions: Use recovery plans for multi-tier apps.
Run test failovers regularly and after major changes.
Choose 'Latest processed' for fastest RTO or 'Latest' for lowest data loss.

walkthrough.subtitle: Keep a running copy of your VMs in another region, and switch to it if the main region fails.

steps.label: Region down
steps.title: The whole region is unavailable
body: A backup lets you rebuild, but restoring dozens of VMs takes hours. The business needs to be running again in minutes.

steps.label: DR
steps.title: Disaster recovery keeps a warm copy
body: Azure Site Recovery (ASR) replicates VM disks continuously to another region. Recovery point objective (RPO): how much data you might lose, usually seconds to minutes. Recovery time objective (RTO): how long until you are running again.

steps.label: Test
steps.title: Practise with a test failover
body: A test failover creates VMs from a recovery point in an isolated network you choose, without stopping replication or touching production. Check the app, then 'Cleanup test failover'.

callout.text: Always use a separate, isolated VNet for test failovers.

steps.label: Failover
steps.title: The real thing
body: Failover creates VMs in the target region from a recovery point. Commit makes it final. Re-protect starts replicating back the other way, so later you can fail back.

steps.label: Plans
steps.title: Recovery plans
body: A recovery plan groups VMs and sets their order (database first, then app, then web), with scripts or manual steps between groups.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Site Recovery
body: Replicate, test, fail over, commit, re-protect.
recap: Backup = restore later; ASR = switch over quickly
Vault in the target region; continuous replication
Test failover into an isolated VNet, then clean up

handsOn.title: Replicate a VM to another region and run a test failover
handsOn.cost: Low. One B1s VM costs about US$0.01 per hour. Delete the same day. Site Recovery is free for each protected VM for the first 31 days; replicated disks add cents. Allow time: initial replication takes 30–60 minutes.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription (a free or pay-as-you-go account works). Work in a resource group called rg-az104-lab.
If rg-az104-lab does not exist yet: search 'Resource groups' > Create > name rg-az104-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

A small Linux VM vm-lab in rg-az104-lab: Virtual machines > + Create, Ubuntu 24.04, Standard_B1s, password authentication, public inbound ports None. If the VM cannot reach the internet later, its subnet is private (the default for new networks): open the virtual network > Subnets, untick 'Enable private subnet', save, then stop and start the VM. In production use a NAT gateway instead. Monitoring agents, Azure Backup and Site Recovery all need to reach Azure services.
Pick a second region for the copy, for example UAE Central if your subscription can use it, or another nearby region.

steps.do: Open vm-lab > Operations > Disaster recovery. Target region: your second region. Review the advanced settings: target resource group, VNet, cache storage. Review + Start replication.
steps.see: A job enabling replication. Azure creates a vault and target resources for you.

steps.do: Wait until vm-lab > Disaster recovery shows Replication health: Healthy and status Protected (30–60 minutes).
steps.see: A map with source and target regions and the latest recovery points.

steps.do: Create a VNet in the target region named vnet-test (any range) for the test failover.
On vm-lab > Disaster recovery select Test failover. Recovery point: Latest processed. Azure virtual network: vnet-test. OK.
steps.see: A test failover job. A new VM named like vm-lab-test appears in the target region.
It is running in the target region, in vnet-test. Production vm-lab is untouched.

steps.do: Back on vm-lab > Disaster recovery select Cleanup test failover, tick 'Testing is complete', OK.
steps.see: The test VM is deleted. Replication continues.

steps.do: Read the Failover and Commit buttons, but do not run a real failover.

check: A test failover VM ran in the target region and was cleaned up.
cleanup: Delete the resource groups Site Recovery created in the target region (names ending in -asr) and vnet-test.
When you finish for the day: Resource groups > rg-az104-lab > Delete resource group > type the name > Delete. This removes everything inside it.
